metadata.file_name: Euro J of Education - 2025 - Ye - Exploring the Relationship Between Students  Physical Activity and Academic Achievement.pdf
metadata.title: Exploring the Relationship Between Students' Physical Activity and Academic Achievement in Different Social Environments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata and draws a two-stage stratified sample of schools and students, then applies the weighting variables provided by PISA to address unequal selection probabilities after sampling stages. The authors report that they weighted the sample using PISA-provided weighting variables and supplemented missing variables using multiple interpolations to finalize the analytic dataset. The manuscript does not name a specific PISA weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT), so the exact weight field cannot be identified from the text. Because the analysis is conducted with OLS and includes school fixed effects, the weighting is intended to improve representativeness under the complex survey design, but the paper does not report replicate-weight variance estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 student data for 15-year-olds (grades 7 and above) and sampled 397,388 students from 52 countries and territories. The authors applied a multi-step refinement: (1) selected regions with sufficiently large student samples, (2) excluded regions composed exclusively of either developed or developing countries to preserve a balanced comparative frame, and (3) aggregated territories that are administratively part of the same sovereign country into a single national dataset. They also note omissions in needed variables and addressed these by weighting with PISA-provided weights and supplementing missing data via multiple interpolations (maximum 5 iterations). No further grade- or school-type restriction is described beyond the PISA target population and the region/country refinement steps.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Mathematics achievement the study leveraged Moderate activity days (MPA), Vigorous activity days (VPA), Exercise before school (EBS), Exercise after school (EAS), and Physical education days (PES) to predict Math achievement, finding that MPA was positively associated (β=0.048) while VPA (β=−0.020), PES (β=−0.031), and EBS (β=−0.124) were negatively associated; EAS was positive but small (β=0.033). This indicates that policies promoting moderate out-of-school physical activity may align with higher academic performance, while high-intensity activity and more frequent PE classes may require careful scheduling to avoid time trade-offs or fatigue effects, though the study reports associations rather than causal effects.

Using PISA 2015 Reading achievement the study leveraged Moderate activity days (MPA), Vigorous activity days (VPA), Exercise before school (EBS), Exercise after school (EAS), and Physical education days (PES) to predict Reading achievement, finding that MPA was positively associated (β=0.067) while VPA (β=−0.027), PES (β=−0.040), and EBS (β=−0.158) were negatively associated; EAS was positive but small (β=0.031). This indicates that strengthening moderate physical activity opportunities may support reading outcomes, while increasing PE frequency or vigorous activity—especially before school—may be counterproductive without balancing academic time and managing fatigue, noting the paper’s correlational OLS framework.

Using PISA 2015 Science achievement the study leveraged Moderate activity days (MPA), Vigorous activity days (VPA), Exercise before school (EBS), Exercise after school (EAS), and Physical education days (PES) to predict Science achievement, finding that MPA was positively associated (β=0.063) while VPA (β=−0.026), PES (β=−0.041), and EBS (β=−0.154) were negatively associated; EAS was positive but small (β=0.035). This indicates that moderate out-of-school physical activity may be a promising complement to science learning, whereas frequent PE and vigorous activity—particularly before school—may require policy attention to avoid negative time/fatigue trade-offs, with causality not established.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 student data (397,388 students across 52 countries/territories) to examine how physical activity intensity and timing relate to academic achievement in mathematics, reading, and science. Using OLS regressions with school fixed effects and PISA-provided weighting, the authors report statistically significant associations (Table 3) where moderate physical activity outside school (MPA) is positively related to achievement (Math β=0.048; Read β=0.067; Science β=0.063; all p<0.01), while vigorous activity (VPA) and physical education days (PES) are negatively related (e.g., Math VPA β=−0.020; PES β=−0.031). Exercise before school (EBS) shows the strongest negative associations across subjects (Math β=−0.124; Read β=−0.158; Science β=−0.154). The paper emphasizes cross-context heterogeneity (Tables 4–6) and explicitly notes that results reflect correlations rather than causality; it also does not provide replicate-weight uncertainty estimates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript is an econometric OLS analysis of associations using PISA 2015, not a machine-learning predictive modeling study. As a result, no ML algorithms are evaluated (ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty) and the extraction focuses on regression-based findings rather than ML performance. The paper also does not report plausible-value (PV) handling explicitly; given that PISA achievement is PV-based, the extraction assumes standard PV-based achievement scoring, but the exact PV procedure is not documented.
